# Limit Check Overflow

This example demonstrates a subtle arithmetic bug in a defensive limit check.

The code appears to reserve space safely before processing inbound data, but
the validation is still wrong because an intermediate integer calculation
overflows before the result is widened to `long`.

That is the secure-coding lesson: choosing a wider destination type is not
enough if the dangerous arithmetic already happened in a narrower type.

## What you will learn

By the end of this example you will understand:

- why `int + int` is still an `int` in Java even if the result is assigned to a `long`
- how an overflow in validation logic can turn a reject path into an accept path
- why length values coming from a remote system must be treated as untrusted
- how to structure the calculation so the limit check remains monotonic and safe
- why explicit vulnerable and fixed variants are easier to review than an in-place edit

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 21 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

This example uses the Maven Wrapper (`./mvnw`), so you do not need to install
Maven separately.

## Build the example

Compile the example before running the vulnerable and fixed variants.

We use `compile` here because the lesson is about arithmetic and control flow,
not about packaging. Compiling once gives you the classes under
`target/classes`, which keeps the walkthrough fast and focused.

What you gain from this step: a clean baseline for comparing the unsafe and safe
implementations.

```shell
./mvnw clean compile
```

Build output

```
...
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
...
```

## Inspect the vulnerable code

Start with the vulnerable implementation.

The application wants to protect a fictional buffer with a maximum capacity of
`10_000`. It retrieves a header length and a body length from a remote service
and rejects the input if there is no space left.

What you gain from this step: you see the exact line where a reasonable-looking
limit check becomes unsafe.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.limit_check;

import java.nio.BufferOverflowException;

public final class App {
    private static final long MAX_BUFFER_CAPACITY = 10_000;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // BUG: both operands are int, so this addition overflows before the result
        // is widened to long.
        long inbound = RemoteServiceProxy.headerLength() + RemoteServiceProxy.bodyLength();

        long available = MAX_BUFFER_CAPACITY - inbound;

        if (available < 0) {
            System.err.println("I'm out of buffer! Available space = " + available);
            throw new BufferOverflowException();
        }

        // do stuff
        System.out.println("I'm doing stuff!\n");
        System.out.println("available buffer space = " + available);
    }
}
```

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.limit_check;

public final class RemoteServiceProxy {
    public static int headerLength() {
        return 20_000;
    }

    public static int bodyLength() {
        return Integer.MAX_VALUE - 5_000;
    }
}
```

Two details matter:

- the lengths come from a remote source, so they must be treated as untrusted
- `headerLength()` and `bodyLength()` both return `int`

The assignment target is `long`, but that does not make the addition safe. In
Java, `int + int` is evaluated as `int` first. If that intermediate sum
overflows, the damage is already done before the result is stored in `long`.

## Run the vulnerable variant

Now run the vulnerable class.

What you gain from this step: you see the bug as an observable behavior rather
than as an abstract arithmetic rule.

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.limit_check.App
```

Observed output

```
I'm doing stuff!

available buffer space = 2147478649
```

The program claims there is still space available:

- `available buffer space = 2147478649`

That result is impossible because the buffer capacity is only `10_000`.

The overflow happens like this:

- header length = `20_000`
- body length = `2_147_478_647`
- mathematical sum = `2_147_498_647`
- that value does not fit in a signed 32-bit `int`
- the wrapped `int` result becomes negative before it is widened to `long`
- subtracting a negative number makes `available` look huge and positive

This is exactly why limit checks are security-critical code. A single overflow
can invert the decision and allow processing to continue when it should stop.

## Inspect the remediated variant

The fixed version avoids the dangerous intermediate addition entirely.

What you gain from this step: you see a safer structure for the same logic, not
just a warning about what went wrong.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.limit_check;

import java.nio.BufferOverflowException;

public final class App_fixed {
    private static final long MAX_BUFFER_CAPACITY = 10_000;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Each subtraction is performed in long arithmetic because the left-hand
        // operand is already a long.
        long available = MAX_BUFFER_CAPACITY - RemoteServiceProxy.headerLength() - RemoteServiceProxy.bodyLength();

        if (available < 0) {
            System.err.println("I'm out of buffer! Available space = " + available);
            throw new BufferOverflowException();
        }

        // do stuff
        System.out.println("I'm doing stuff!\n");
        System.out.println("available buffer space = " + available);
    }
}
```

## Run the remediated variant

Run the fixed variant and compare the outcome.

What you gain from this step: you confirm that the corrected arithmetic now
drives the program into the reject path.

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.limit_check.App_fixed
```

Expected failure

```
I'm out of buffer! Available space = -2147488647
Exception in thread "main" java.nio.BufferOverflowException
	at com.oracle.jsc.limit_check.App_fixed.main(App_fixed.java:15)
```

This time the program rejects the input because the remaining capacity is
negative and the limit check finally behaves as intended.

The important design point is not merely "use `long`". The more defensible rule
is:

- make sure the arithmetic is performed in a safe type from the start
- avoid combining large untrusted values in a narrow intermediate expression
- keep the limit check easy to audit, because validation arithmetic is part of
  your security boundary

## What this example teaches

- Validation code can fail open when arithmetic overflows.
- Assigning to `long` does not help if the expression already overflowed as `int`.
- Lengths and sizes from remote systems are untrusted data and must be handled defensively.
- A safer structure is often simpler to review than a clever compact expression.
- Secure coding includes reasoning about numeric types, not only about strings and input formats.
